column2: Seeing this great deed, the sages who speak of Brahman, smiling at one another, bowed to the Supreme Person.
Vishnu, the Self of all beings, having taken the dwarf form and bewildering the whole world, went to the forest for austerity.
Such is the power of the goddess Ganga, born from Vishnu's foot, by whose mere remembrance one is freed from all sins.
Whoever reads or hears this greatness of the Ganga in a temple or on a riverbank gains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
He who always does good to Brahmins has performed all sacrifices; he has bathed in all holy places and performed all austerity.
He who urges another to give "Give!" to support Brahmins also obtains that fruit; what use are other long speeches?
He who has a tank made, himself or through another — his merit cannot be counted even in a life of a hundred years.
If even one traveller drinks the water of a tank, O king, all the sins of its maker are destroyed, without doubt.
Even if a man brings out water lying in the earth for a single day, he is freed from all sins and dwells in heaven for a hundred years.
A mortal who helps another to make a tank, according to his ability, also gets that fruit; so does the one who is pleased and the one who urges.
He who throws out from a tank even a mustard-seed's worth of clay stays in heaven a hundred years, freed from ten million sins.
He with whom the gods or the teachers are pleased, O best of kings, shares the merit of a tank: this is the eternal tradition.
O best of kings, I shall tell you an ancient story, hearing which one is freed from all sins, without doubt.
In the land of Gauda there was a famous king named Virabhadraka, mighty, learned and always honouring Brahmins,
possessed of Vedic learning and the conduct of good families, a friend of poets. His queen, of great fortune, was named Champakamanjari.
That king's great ministers, who deliberated on what should and should not be done, always made decisions on dharma according to the dharma-scriptures.
Whoever speaks on expiation, medicine, astrology and dharma decisions without the scriptures is called a slayer of Brahmins.
Having resolved this in his mind, the king always heard in due order the dharmas taught by Manu and others from his teachers.
No one in his kingdom followed injustice, not even the lowest. In that country protected by dharma under the king,
a likeness to heaven arose, bringing the welfare of good government. Once that king went hunting in a great forest,
surrounded by ministers and others, and wandered till midday. By chance, empty-handed from the hunt and very tired,
the king came upon a lake. Seeing that lake dry, he thought:
Who made this lake on the earth? How can water be had here, by which this king may live?
Then the idea came to him, O best of kings: having dug a hole a cubic deep in it, he got water.
By drinking that water the king's thirst was quenched, and also that of the minister named Buddhisagara.
Buddhisagara, knower of dharma and wealth, said to the king: "O king, this lake once held rain-water.
Today the idea has come to me to have it walled and banked. May you be pleased, O lord, and give me your command, O sinless one."
Hearing the minister's words, the best of kings rejoiced greatly, ready to do it himself.
He appointed that same minister to the meritorious work. Then, by the king's order, Buddhisagara with joy,
the greatest doer of merit, set about making the lake like an ocean: fifty bow-lengths wide in all directions.
He built the lake, bound with stone and fathomlessly deep, and having completed it reported everything to the king.
From then on all forest-dwellers and thirsty travellers got good water there, O king.
Once, at the end of his life, that minister Buddhisagara died and came to the world of the one who rules the world — me, O lord (Yama speaks).
I asked about him, and Chitragupta, the writer of dharma's ledger, told me all his deeds.
He himself was the counsellor in the king's work of dharma; therefore he deserves to board the aerial car of dharma.
When Chitragupta said so, I ordered Buddhisagara to board the car called Dharma.
Then, after some time, O king, King Virabhadraka died and came to my abode, and I greeted him with joy.
There too I asked about all his deeds, and Chitragupta told me the dharma arising from the lake.
Then I instructed the king properly; hear how. On a sandy hill by the shore, O king,
a lapwing dug with its beak two finger-breadths for water. Then in time a boar
dug a cubit with its snout and got water. Then another day a deer dug two cubits.
Having dug into the water, O great king, water stood for two months and was drunk by small forest creatures troubled by thirst.
Then after three years an elephant by its trunk dug three cubits, and more water came.
That water stood three months and was drunk by forest creatures; then you came there after the water had dried up.
You dug a cubit and got water there, O king; then, by your minister's counsel,
fifty bows were dug and a great water arose; again it was firmly bound with stones and became a great lake, and trees were planted there, benefiting all the world.
By his own merit each of these five, O lord of the earth, has boarded the car of dharma; you too board it.
Hearing my words, that king boarded the car; he was the sixth, sharing an equal part (of merit).
Thus I have told you all of the fruit born of a tank; hearing it, one is freed from sin from birth to death.
The man who with faith hears or reads this account obtains all the merit born of making a lake.
One who sprinkles the ground with water also attains heaven. He who sprinkles the ground of a temple with scented water
remains near the god for as many ages as there are drops. He who plasters a temple with clay or mineral pastes
uplifts ten million of his family and attains likeness to Vishnu (slayer of Madhu). The mortal who whitewashes a shrine with powdered stone,
or makes auspicious signs like the svastika, gains endless merit. O king, he who arranges lamps in a temple —
I cannot count his merit even in a hundred years. He who keeps an unbroken lamp for Vishnu or Shankara
gets the fruit of a horse-sacrifice at every moment, not hard to attain. He who sees Shankara or Vishnu worshipped and bows
reaches Vishnu's abode and rejoices there for ten thousand ages. One circumambulation of the Goddess, seven of the Sun, O king,
three of Vinayaka and four in a temple of Vishnu: having done these, one reaches that deity's house and rejoices a hundred thousand ages.
He who circumambulates Vishnu with devotion, or a cow or a Brahmin, gets a horse-sacrifice at every step.
He who in Kashi worships and bows to the Linga of Maheshvara has no duty left and is not born again in samsara.
A man who circumambulates Shiva by the right, properly, does not fall from heaven by Shankara's grace.
One who praises Narayana, lord of the world, the faultless, with hymns obtains all desires, whatever he wishes in mind.
He who, full of devotion, dances or sings in a temple, O king, is a partaker of liberation in the world of Rudra.
Men who play instruments in a temple mount swan-chariots and go to Brahma's abode.
Those who clap their hands in a temple are freed from all sins and stay in an aerial car for ten thousand ages.
Even Shiva himself is unable to declare the merit of those who ring bells in a temple.
Hear the fruit of merit of those who please the Lord of gods with drums, mridangas, tabors, and dindima.
Joined with hosts of divine women and honoured with all desires, they reach heaven and rejoice for five kalpas.
A man who sounds a conch in a temple, O king, is freed from all sins and rejoices with Vishnu.
A man who makes the sound of cymbals and gongs in Vishnu's house is freed from all sins and attains Vishnu's world.
The God Vishnu, who sees all, of the nature of knowledge, stainless, being pleased gives full fruit of all dharma.
By the mere remembrance of him, the God of gods who bears the discus, all actions become fruitful, O king.
The Supreme Self, Lord of the world, giver of the fruit of all actions, who destroys all distress, is always remembered by doers of good; whatever is done with reference to him becomes endless.
Vishnu is the dharmas, Vishnu the fruits; Vishnu the actions and the enjoyer of fruits; Vishnu is the work and the instruments; nothing exists apart from him.
One who kills himself by rope or other means: when dead, he is to be smeared with impure matter (as penance); for one still living, the fine is two hundred.
